summary: The oldest thing on this map and by far the widest. A published international standard, fourth edition, whose forty-two clauses already contain most of what newer formats are still drafting: rigid body physics with six joint types, spatialized sound with room acoustics, a human skeleton standard, text with fonts, volume rendering, shader bindings, a geospatial component with real coordinate reference frames, an event model for interactivity, a scripting component, and a networked component that shares entity state over a long-established simulation protocol. It also carries a proper conformance clause, which almost nothing else here does. Levels below say native for anything defined in a clause of this standard, since components are how this standard is built; where support depends on which profile a reader implements, the note says so. Three warnings for a standards audience. Its coverage is wide but its adoption is thin, so a cell being filled here does not mean two shipping products interoperate. Its unit of length can be changed by the file, unlike the common asset format, which fixes metres. And its addressing points at a file, not at a shared place, so two people opening the same address get two private copies.

coverage.note: Clause 4 defines the scene graph, the transformation hierarchy and the rules for ancestors and descendants, including that a node may not be its own ancestor.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4 Concepts
sources.quote: X3D includes the notion of local coordinate systems , defined in terms of transformations from ancestor coordinate systems. The coordinate system in which the root nodes are displayed is called the world coordinate system .

coverage.note: One fixed convention, right-handed with the vertical axis up, stated in the concepts clause. It matches the common asset format, which makes exchange between them straightforward.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4.3.6 Standard units and coordinate system
sources.quote: ISO/IEC 19775 uses a Cartesian, right-handed, three-dimensional coordinate system. By default, the viewer is on the Z-axis looking down the -Z-axis toward the origin with +X to the right and +Y straight up.

coverage.note: Metres by default, with base units for angle, force, mass and time each tied to an international units standard. Unlike the common asset format, a file may declare a different length unit, so a reader must honour the declaration rather than assume metres.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4.3.6 Standard units and coordinate system
sources.quote: ISO/IEC 19775 defines the initial base unit of measure of the world coordinate system to be metres. However, the world coordinate units may be modified by specifying a different length unit using the UNIT statement.

coverage.note: The architecture part defines the scene contents; the byte-level encodings that carry them sit in a companion part of the same standard, not in this document. Cite the encodings separately if the question is about file bytes.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: This document is Edition 4 of ISO/IEC 19775-1, Extensible 3D (X3D).

coverage.note: Three separate clauses cover rendering primitives, three-dimensional geometry and two-dimensional geometry, with a further clause for engineering geometry.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: Geometry3D component provides a detailed specification of the Geometry3D component of X3D.

coverage.note: A texturing clause plus separate clauses for three-dimensional textures, cube maps and texture projection.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: Texturing component provides a detailed specification of the Texturing component of X3D including advanced material characteristics.

coverage.note: The physically based material node was deliberately aligned with the common asset format's material, and the standard says so in a note. This is the clearest worked example on the whole map of two standards bodies making an exchange lossless on purpose.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 12.4.6 PhysicalMaterial
sources.quote: The physical material properties of X3D are also deliberately consistent with the glTF 2.0 material definition. Effectively, converting (in either direction) between X3D PhysicalMaterial and glTF 2.0 material definitions is equivalent.

coverage.note: Animation is expressed as interpolator nodes driven by a time sensor and wired to targets by routes, rather than as a clip. That makes it flexible inside the file and awkward to lift out as a portable clip.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: Interpolation component provides a detailed specification of the Interpolation component of X3D.

coverage.note: The humanoid animation clause defines a joint, a segment and an attachment site, giving a bone hierarchy with defined semantics rather than an anonymous tree.

sources.quote: 26.3.1 HAnimDisplacer 26.3.2 HAnimHumanoid 26.3.3 HAnimJoint 26.3.4 HAnimMotion 26.3.5 HAnimSegment 26.3.6 HAnimSite

coverage.note: The displacer node moves a named set of vertices by a list of offsets, which is a blend shape by another name, and is how facial detail is carried.

coverage.note: The humanoid clause binds a separate international standard for humanoid animation into this one, so bone names and structure are agreed rather than left to convention. This is the answer that the common asset format still lacks.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 26.1.2 Overview
sources.quote: The HAnim component of X3D defines the node bindings and other specifics for implementing ISO/IEC 19774 (see [I19774] ) within X3D.

coverage.note: A humanoid node gathers the joints, segments and sites into one figure, which is the portable description of a body. It does not specify clothing, wearables or expression sets.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 26.2 Concepts
sources.quote: This component maps the functionality defined in ISO/IEC 19774 to a set of X3D nodes. The semantics for these nodes are as specified therein.

coverage.note: Clause 37 defines rigid bodies and rigid body collections. It is in the fullest profile, so a reader may conform to the standard without implementing it.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 37 Rigid body physics component
sources.quote: Only the subset of the laws of physics known as rigid body physics is supported.

coverage.note: Collidable shapes and offsets, collision spaces, collision collections, a collision sensor and a contact node, kept separate from the visible geometry.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 37.4 Node reference
sources.quote: 37.4.2 CollidableOffset 37.4.3 CollidableShape 37.4.4 CollisionCollection 37.4.5 CollisionSensor 37.4.6 CollisionSpace 37.4.7 Contact

coverage.note: Six joint types: ball, single-axis hinge, double-axis hinge, motor, slider and universal, with range-of-motion limits and a defined breaking behaviour.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 37.2.3 Joints
sources.quote: A joint is used to connect two bodies together in a way that imposes a set of constraints on the movement of the two bodies relative to one another. Many different joint types are provided

They attach to the collision collection and to contacts rather than to a surface, which is a different shape of answer from a per-material approach and will not map across one for one.

coverage.note: A proximity sensor fires on entering and leaving a box, with the entry timestamped exactly. It watches the viewer; a separate sensor watches objects. There is no general trigger volume attached to an arbitrary rigid body.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 22.4.1 ProximitySensor
sources.quote: The ProximitySensor node generates events when the viewer enters, exits, and moves within a region in space (defined by a box).

coverage.note: Sound sources include recorded clips, buffers, microphones, oscillators and network streams, each placed in the scene with a location and a direction.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 16.2.1 Audio and sound spatial architecture
sources.quote: The Sound and SpatialSound nodes define location, direction, and characteristics of expected sound production in virtual 3D space.

coverage.note: Clause 16 covers spatialized sound and acoustic rendering, with listening points that can sit anywhere and face any direction.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 16.2.1 Audio and sound spatial architecture
sources.quote: The Sound component provides a rich set of spatialized audio capabilities in a comprehensive architecture suitable for 3D models and virtual environments.

coverage.note: Acoustic properties attach to geometry and colour the sound, and a set of processing nodes including convolution, filtering, delay and compression let a space be given a character.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 16.2.1 and 16.4 Node reference
sources.quote: Attenuation characteristics may be further modified by AcousticProperties in the Shape component describing reflection, refraction and absorption that affect sound-propagation interactions with surrounding geometry.

coverage.note: The propagation model covers reflection, refraction and absorption against surrounding geometry, which is most of the physical picture. What is missing is the words themselves: occlusion and obstruction never appear in the clause, and no algorithm is specified for a sound blocked by a wall, so two readers may treat that case differently.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 16.2.1 Audio and sound spatial architecture
sources.quote: Attenuation characteristics may be further modified by AcousticProperties in the Shape component describing reflection, refraction and absorption that affect sound-propagation interactions with surrounding geometry.

coverage.note: There are nodes for a streamed audio source and a streamed audio destination, so the scene can say where live audio enters and leaves. What is missing is the wire: no transport, no codec negotiation and no scale behaviour are specified.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 16.4 Node reference
sources.quote: 16.4.19 StreamAudioDestination 16.4.20 StreamAudioSource

coverage.note: A text node with a font style node covering family, style, direction, justification and language. Text is turned into geometry, so it is legible in three dimensions rather than pasted on as an image.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 15 Text component
sources.quote: The Text component specifies how text strings are rendered in an X3D scene.

coverage.note: Named viewpoints in perspective or orthographic form, only one bound at a time, plus a navigation information node that says how the user may move. Viewpoints are addressable, which is what makes deep links into a scene possible.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 23 Navigation component
sources.quote: This document specifies two node types derived from X3DViewpointNode . The Viewpoint node specifies a perspective viewpoint while the OrthoViewpoint node specifies an orth

coverage.note: A level-of-detail node switches representations by distance, and the geospatial clause adds a terrain form of it that also loads and unloads children.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 23.4.3 LOD and clause 25.3.4 GeoLOD
sources.quote: The GeoLOD node provides a terrain-specialized form of the LOD node.

coverage.note: A dedicated clause gives the lighting equations and the shadow requirements, so the standard says how a lit surface should look rather than leaving it to each reader.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: Lighting component defines lighting and shadow requirements for visually rendering X3D models.

coverage.note: Clause 41 covers rendering volumetric data sets inside a scene, which no other subject on the asset side of this map has in a ratified form.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: Volume rendering component provides a detailed specification for the rendering of volumetric data sets as part of X3D worlds.

coverage.note: A programmable shaders clause with three named shading language bindings in the annexes. This is the opposite choice from the common asset format, which stays deliberately neutral. Shader source in a file is by nature not portable across graphics interfaces.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 Architecture, contents
sources.quote: 31 Programmable shaders component

sources.quote: I OpenGL shading language (GLSL) binding

coverage.note: Every node that carries geographic coordinates has a field naming its spatial reference frame, with geodetic, transverse mercator and geocentric forms, a table of ellipsoids and a geoid for mean sea level.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 25.2.3 Specifying a spatial reference frame
sources.quote: All the X3D nodes that allow inclusion of geographic coordinates support a field called geoSystem . This field is used to specify the particular spatial reference frame that will be used for the geospatial coordinates in that node.

coverage.note: A geographic location node places content at a point on the Earth and orients it to the local frame, with the vertical axis up and one horizontal axis pointing north. Note it defines its own way of saying this rather than referencing the separate pose standard from the geospatial consortium.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 25.3.3 GeoLocation
sources.quote: axis is the up direction for that local area (the normal to the tangent plane on the ellipsoid), −Z points towards the north pole, and +X is east.

coverage.note: A terrain level-of-detail node holds up to four child addresses in a quadtree and manages loading and unloading, which is tiled terrain streaming written into an international standard long before the tiled formats in current use.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 25.3.4 GeoLOD
sources.quote: The GeoLOD node provides a terrain-specialized form of the LOD node. It is a grouping node that specifies two different levels of detail for an object using a tree structure, where 0 to 4 children can be specified

coverage.note: Interactivity travels inside the file as a graph of one-way connections between fields, changeable while running, with a defined propagation order. This is a ratified answer to the same question the common asset format is still trying to ratify.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4.3.7 Behaviour graph
sources.quote: The event model of X3D allows the declaration of unidirectional ROUTE connections between fields and a model for the propagation of events along those connections.

coverage.note: Clause 29 defines a script node with an initialize and shutdown lifecycle, event handling and field access. The language bindings themselves live in a companion part of the standard.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 29 Scripting component
sources.quote: This includes how Script nodes are used to effect changes in X3D worlds.

coverage.note: Some real precautions are written into the text: a model may not include itself, directly or indirectly, and readers are told not to honour such loops; automatic reloading carries an explicit warning. What is missing is everything general. There is no isolation model for scripts, no permission model and no resource budget, so a scene that runs a script is trusting it.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 9.4.2 Inline
sources.quote: X3D browsers shall not honor self-referential loading of Inline model loops in order to avoid security vulnerabilities.

coverage.note: Clause 28 binds a long-standing distributed simulation protocol into the scene, with entity state, transmitter, receiver and signal messages. Two cautions: it shares platform-level simulation entities, not general world state, and it lives in the fullest profile only. It is nonetheless a ratified international standard for sharing state between running instances, which the rest of this map does not have.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 28 Distributed interactive simulation component
sources.quote: The Distributed Interactive Simulation (DIS) component provides networked interoperability with the IEEE DIS protocol (see [IEEE1278] and [SISO] ) for sharing state and conducting real-time platform-level simulations across multiple host computers.

coverage.note: A scene can pull in another file, and named values can be imported and exported across that boundary; prototypes let a definition live in a separate file. What is missing is override: there is no way for one source to change a value inside another, and no layering with a strength order. That is the gap the scene description standard was built to fill.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 9.4.2 Inline
sources.quote: it is an error for a model to Inline itself, directly or indirectly, in order to avoid nonterminating recursion loops

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4.4.5 External prototype semantics
sources.quote: 4.4.5 External prototype semantics 4.4.5.1 Introduction 4.4.5.2 EXTERNPROTO interface semantics 4.4.5.3 EXTERNPROTO URL semantics 4.4.6 Import/Export semantics

coverage.note: An anchor node replaces the current world with another one fetched from an address, so plain traversal between worlds is ratified and has been for years. What is missing is everything that should travel with you: no identity, no appearance and no possessions cross the jump.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 9.4.1 Anchor
sources.quote: If the URL points to a valid X3D file, that world replaces the world of which the Anchor node is a part

coverage.note: Addresses name a file on a server, not a live shared place. Two people opening the same address get two independent copies with no connection between them. Nothing resolves a place name into a joinable destination.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 9.2.1 URLs, URNs and URIs
sources.quote: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a form of Universal Resource Identifier (URI) described in [URI] [RFC8089] that specifies a file located on a particular server and accessed through a specified protocol

coverage.note: A whole clause on conformance, separately for files, generators and readers, with a base profile that sets minimum requirements and stated aims of eliminating arbitrary subsets and promoting uniform tests. Very little else on this map has this.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 6 Conformance
sources.quote: to promote interoperability by eliminating arbitrary subsets of, or extensions to, ISO/IEC 19775; to promote uniformity in the development of conformance tests

coverage.note: Nothing survives a restart because nothing is ever written back. The standard's own list of what an X3D application does covers the world coordinate space, the objects in it, hyperlinks, behaviours and connection to external code, and stops there; there is no store, no save, and no notion of a world that is resumed. The two places the word persistent appears both mean the state of a node's fields while the scene is running, not across a restart. Clause 28 shares live entity state between hosts and keeps none of it. Checked clauses 4 Concepts, 7 Core, 8 Time, 9 Networking, 28 Distributed interactive simulation and 29 Scripting.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4.1.2 Overview
sources.quote: Each X3D application: implicitly establishes a world coordinate space for all objects defined, as well as all objects included by the application; explicitly defines and composes a set of 2D, 3D and multimedia objects; can specify hyperlinks to other files and applications; can define object behaviours; can connect to external modules or applications via programming and scripting languages.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 29.2.10 Accessing fields and events
sources.quote: The field values can be read or written and are persistent across method call, and changes to a field can notify the node through its update method.

coverage.note: There is one settings vocabulary in the standard and it does not belong to the user. Clause 9.2.4 names nine browser options, among them antialiasing, shading mode, render quality while moving and texture quality, passed in at start-up and held either as parameters on the embedding tag or, in the standard's own words, in an application-specific configuration file or registry entry. Support for them is recommended rather than required, none of them is an accessibility choice, nothing ties a setting to a person, and nothing carries one to another world or another reader. Navigation type, viewpoint and headlight settings in clause 23 belong to the scene, and the reader's own interface for them is explicitly left implementation-dependent. Checked clauses 4 Concepts, 7 Core, 9 Networking, 23 Navigation and 24 Environmental effects.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 9.2.4 X3D browser options
sources.quote: Browser options may be set as HTML PARAM values within an EMBED or OBJECT tag if the X3D browser is running as an embedded control within a World Wide Web browser, or through an application-specific mechanism such as a configuration file or system registry entry if the X3D browser is running within some other containing application. Support for X3D browser options is not required but is strongly recommended.

coverage.note: Half of this is answered, and answered by name. An HAnimSite is a grouping node whose stated second purpose is an attachment point for accessories such as jewelry and clothing; it takes children, so a hat or a strap hangs beneath it, and the humanoid node keeps a list of its sites. The names come from the humanoid animation standard that this clause binds in, so the same point means the same thing in two files from two authors, which is more than the common asset format offers. What is missing is the item. Nothing defines a wearable as a separate thing that can move from one avatar to another, there are no fitting or scaling rules for bodies of different shape, there is no ownership, and there is no way to put something on or take it off. A garment travels only inside the humanoid that already carries it.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 26.3.6 HAnimSite
sources.quote: An HAnimSite node serves three purposes. The first is to define an "end effecter" location that can be used by an inverse kinematics system. The second is to define an attachment point for accessories such as jewelry and clothing.

coverage.note: Nothing in the forty-two clauses asks for or presents a credential. The words credential, authentication, certificate, password and authorization do not occur anywhere in this part; permission and privacy occur once each, in a single security sentence on the microphone node that hands the question to the host application. The only identifiers the standard itself defines are simulation numbers in clause 28, a site, an application and an entity, and those are allocation conventions inside one exercise rather than proof of who anyone is. Checked clauses 6 Conformance, 7 Core, 9 Networking including the browser options table, 16 Sound, 28 Distributed interactive simulation and 29 Scripting.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 16.4.14 MicrophoneSource
sources.quote: Security consideration: enabling a MicrophoneSource node has privacy and permission prerequisites.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 28.2.3 Common DIS fields
sources.quote: The intent for each simulation exercise is for each DIS site to be assigned a unique identifier, and each simulation application at a DIS site assigned an application identifier unique within that site.

coverage.note: The time half is specified better here than in most of this map. Zero is midnight Greenwich time on 1 January 1970, absolute times are seconds in double precision, a whole clause defines the reader's clock and the nodes that follow it, processing an event at a given time may only produce events at that time or later, and everything in one event cascade carries the same timestamp and is treated as simultaneous. Ordering inside one reader is therefore exact and written down. The shared half is absent. The clock is that reader's own, the one networked clause stamps an arriving message with the moment it reached the local machine, and nothing in the standard agrees a clock between two hosts, estimates the offset between them or orders events across them.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 8.2.2 Time origin
sources.quote: Time (0.0) is equivalent to 00:00:00 GMT January 1, 1970. Absolute times are specified in SFTime or MFTime fields as double-precision floating point numbers representing seconds.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 4.4.8.3 Execution model
sources.quote: All events generated during a given event cascade are assigned the same timestamp as the initial event, since all are considered to happen instantaneously.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 clause 28.2.3 Common DIS fields
sources.quote: The timestamp field provides the time (SFTime) at which the DIS message arrived, referenced to local system time.

coverage.note: X3D's sensors read pointing devices, keys, time, proximity and collision. The viewer is described to the browser as a size and a speed, not read as a face or a body pose, and there is no live sensor stream of the person to hand to the scene.

sources.title: X3D 4.0 (ISO/IEC 19775-1) Part 1, Navigation component
sources.quote: The NavigationInfo node contains information describing the physical characteristics of the viewer's avatar and viewing model.

coverage.note: The strongest declaration of navigable space in any file format on this map, and still only half the row. NavigationInfo carries the avatar's size and the navigation paradigm the browser must present, WALK among them, and Viewpoint nodes give named places a visitor can be put down at, all of it inside the file. What is missing is the walkable surface itself: X3D has no navigation mesh, and the ground a body may stand on is worked out by the browser from Collision and geometry.

coverage.note: X3D describes a scene and how a browser runs it. It has no publishing service, so there is no path between finished content and an audience for a review to stand in.
X3D's geospatial component places scene content in a geographic frame. It never declares that a map of a place exists, gives it a version, or publishes a transform to a second map of the same place.
An X3D scene is content, not a service that answers for an area. Its geospatial nodes fix where content sits, not which region a service or dataset applies to.
PROTO and EXTERNPROTO define named node interfaces and implementation references, with initial-value and event behavior before a required external implementation becomes available.

coverage.note: X3D's Inline node loads an external X3D scene into the host, and IMPORT/EXPORT statements allow selective event routing between the two via ROUTE. Script nodes in the loaded scene run their own logic. However, events must be explicitly imported and routed one field at a time; there is no automatic bidirectional propagation or consumption protocol. The containment is structural with opt-in routing, not a boundary-aware containment architecture.
